passage:
In the courtyard of their house in a village near Mysuru, Lavanya, twenty months, toddled toward the clay stove where rice was boiling.

"No, Lavanya. Hot," said Kunal Mama firmly, holding up his hand.

She stopped. She looked at the stove, then at his face, then back at the stove. Her lip wobbled. Slowly she turned and walked to the hen instead, glancing back once as if to check he was watching.

"Good girl," he said, and she smiled.

qa.q: What was boiling on the clay stove?
qa.a: Rice was boiling on the stove.

qa.q: What does Lavanya glancing back at Kunal Mama suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was checking his reaction, beginning to sense that the stove was not allowed and wanting his approval.

qa.q: How could Kunal Mama help Lavanya keep learning this rule?
qa.a: He can keep using the same short, firm word, explain "hot" simply, and praise her when she turns away, while still keeping her safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Lavanya when she has to stop?
qa.a: Her wobbling lip shows it was disappointing for her, but his calm face helped her move on.

grounding: Shows a toddler in a village responding to a firm 'no' and sensing that the stove is off limits.

passage:
Lars, two, loved the cat's water bowl in their flat in Tallinn. He splashed it every morning.

"No, Lars. That's Miisu's water," Olga said, moving it.

He looked at her, then crawled straight back and put one finger in, watching her face.

"No," she said again, calm and steady, and lifted him to his own cup. "This one is for you."

The next morning he stood by the bowl, hand hovering, and said, "No!" to himself, then walked away.

qa.q: What did Lars splash every morning?
qa.a: He splashed the cat's water bowl.

qa.q: Why might Lars have put one finger in while watching Olga's face?
qa.a: He seemed to be testing the rule, curious whether she really meant no and what she would do.

qa.q: Why did Olga's way of responding help Lars learn?
qa.a: She stayed calm, repeated the same simple rule and gave him something he was allowed to use instead.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when she sees Lars say "No!" to himself?
qa.a: She would probably feel amused and pleased that her steady approach is working.

grounding: Shows a toddler abroad testing and then starting to follow a simple household prohibition.

passage:
I'm Lalit, Omkar's uncle, visiting from Mumbai. His family speaks Konkani at home, and I don't, much.

At bedtime his Aaji sang the same slow song she sang to his father, rocking him. Omkar, two, hummed along, eyes closing. Next morning at breakfast he pointed at the rice and said a Konkani word I didn't know, and his Aaji beamed. That evening, during aarti, he clapped exactly on the beat.

I can't say what he understands, but it's clearly his.

qa.q: Who sang the bedtime song to Omkar?
qa.a: His Aaji sang it, the same song she sang to his father.

qa.q: What does Aaji's beaming at breakfast suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and happy that Omkar was using the family's home language.

qa.q: How could the family support Omkar's connection to his home language and rituals?
qa.a: They can keep singing, speaking Konkani and including him in daily rituals like aarti, so they stay a natural part of his life.

qa.q: How does Lalit seem to feel as an outsider to the language?
qa.a: He seems a little on the outside but touched, noticing how naturally Omkar belongs to his family's language and songs.

grounding: An uncle observes a toddler absorbing his family's language, lullaby and rituals.

passage:
First week of January: Biji sang a Punjabi folk song while making makki rotis. Gurpreet, two, watched her hands.

A week later: At lunch Gurpreet pointed and said "makki!" Chinmay, his father, grinned. "Biji taught you that?"

Lohri night: Around the bonfire, the aunts started the song. Gurpreet clapped, bounced and shouted the last word of each line. He threw his popcorn into the fire with everyone else, then hugged Biji's knees.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet say at lunch?
qa.a: He pointed and said "makki!"

qa.q: How can you tell Gurpreet felt part of the Lohri celebration?
qa.a: He clapped, bounced, shouted the last words of the song, threw popcorn with everyone and hugged Biji's knees.

qa.q: What small habit helped Gurpreet learn his family's songs and words?
qa.a: Biji singing while she cooked let him hear the language and song again and again in everyday life.

qa.q: What is it like for Biji to see Gurpreet singing at Lohri?
qa.a: She would likely feel joyful and proud that he is taking in the songs she sang.

grounding: Shows a toddler over weeks absorbing a family song, food words and festival ritual.

passage:
"Arohi, it's just the pressure cooker," Jasleen said, but Arohi was already under the table, hands over her ears.

"Too loud! Too loud!"

"Okay, okay." Jasleen crouched. "Want to come to the balcony till it's done?"

Arohi nodded and climbed into her arms.

On the balcony, Arohi's Papa called from inside, "She's so sensitive. Her cousin sleeps through fireworks."

"She's just made differently," Jasleen said. "Next time I'll take her out before the whistle."

qa.q: What sound made Arohi hide under the table?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistle made her hide.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling under the table?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frightened by the loud sound, covering her ears and saying it was too loud.

qa.q: What plan did Jasleen make, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: She decided to take Arohi outside before the whistle next time, which works with Arohi's sensitivity instead of forcing her to endure it.

qa.q: How does Arohi's Papa seem to see her reaction?
qa.a: He compares her to her cousin and seems a bit puzzled or worried that she reacts so strongly.

grounding: A home dialogue shows a toddler's strong sensitivity to noise and an adult adapting to her temperament.

passage:
Note from Vaibhav, playgroup teacher, Monday:

Suraj, two and a half, is our slow-to-warm-up friend. He stands at the door for about ten minutes each morning, watching, before he joins. At music time today he covered his ears when the drum started, but he tapped softly on the table with one finger. Scratchy labels bother him too.

What I did next: I let him watch first, gave him a small soft shaker instead of the drum, and asked his parents about his clothes.

qa.q: What did Suraj do when the drum started?
qa.a: He covered his ears but tapped softly on the table with one finger.

qa.q: What does Suraj's soft tapping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to join the music but felt the drum's loudness was too much for him.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav adjust things for Suraj's temperament?
qa.a: Vaibhav let Suraj watch before joining and gave him a softer shaker, respecting his pace and sensitivity.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents see this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that the teacher understands their son and is working with his needs.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a toddler's cautious, sound- and touch-sensitive temperament and how the teacher adjusted.

passage:
Monday: A cartoon played on the tablet while Mahima cooked. Vijay, two, stared at it, silent, not smiling.

Wednesday: Mahima sat with him and a picture book instead. "Cow! What does a cow say?" Vijay pointed. "Moo!" He turned pages, giggling.

The next weekend: They watched a short video of elephants together. Mahima paused it. "Big ear! Where's your ear?" Vijay grabbed his ear, then trumpeted like an elephant, laughing.

qa.q: What did Mahima and Vijay look at together on Wednesday?
qa.a: They looked at a picture book together.

qa.q: How did Vijay's mood differ between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he stared silently without smiling, while on Wednesday he giggled and joined in, suggesting he enjoyed being with Mahima.

qa.q: What worked about how Mahima used the elephant video?
qa.a: Mahima watched it with him, paused and asked questions, turning the screen into a shared, talking moment.

qa.q: What would change if Vijay only watched cartoons alone?
qa.a: He would miss the back-and-forth talk and play that helped him say words and laugh with Mahima.

grounding: Shows over several days how a toddler learns more through live interaction and shared viewing than a screen alone.

passage:
On Sunday morning in their Lucknow flat, Nitin found a short video of ducks for Ayesha, twenty-two months. He sat her on his lap.

"Duck! Quack quack!" he said. Ayesha flapped her arms. "Quack!"

When it ended she whined for more. Nitin shut the phone. "Let's find a real duck."

They walked to the park pond. When a real duck paddled past, Ayesha squealed and pointed, then looked at him.

"Yes! Duck," he said. She waddled after it, quacking.

qa.q: Where did Nitin and Ayesha go after the video?
qa.a: They walked to the park pond to find a real duck.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel when the video ended, and later at the pond?
qa.a: She was unhappy when it ended and whined for more, but at the pond she was thrilled, squealing and pointing.

qa.q: Which of Nitin's choices helped Ayesha most?
qa.a: Watching together briefly and then taking her to see a real duck turned a short screen moment into live, shared learning.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin when Ayesha whines for more video?
qa.a: It may be tempting to give in, but he chose a better alternative, and her joy at the pond likely made it worth it.

grounding: Shows a parent keeping screen time short and co-viewed, then moving to live interaction.

passage:
Monday: Usha, five, came home from the zoo trip. "Monkey! And ice cream! And the bus!" Bhupen smiled, confused. "Which came first?"

Wednesday: At bedtime he asked about her day. Usha frowned, thinking. "First assembly. Then drawing. Then... lunch. Then I fell."

Saturday: Usha told Nani on the phone about the zoo trip. "First we went on the bus. Then we saw the monkeys. Then we got ice cream. At the end I slept in the bus." Nani laughed. "What a story!" Usha looked at Bhupen, proud.

qa.q: What did Usha say happened at the end of the zoo trip?
qa.a: She said she slept in the bus at the end.

qa.q: Why did Usha look at Bhupen proudly at the end?
qa.a: She felt pleased with herself because she had told the story in order and Nani enjoyed it.

qa.q: What small step helped Usha learn to tell events in order?
qa.a: Bhupen asking "Which came first?" and inviting her to describe her day gave her practice putting events in sequence.

qa.q: How might Nani feel hearing Usha's story?
qa.a: She seemed delighted and entertained, laughing and calling it a great story.

grounding: Shows a young child learning over several days to retell events with a beginning, middle and end.

passage:
The phone line kept breaking, and Ammi was calling from the hospital night shift. Rehana, five, clutched Sangeeta Aunty's phone.

"Ammi, today we... we..." The line crackled. Rehana wanted to say everything at once.

Sangeeta Aunty whispered, "Start with the morning."

Rehana took a breath. "First I brushed teeth. Then Sangeeta Aunty took me to school. Then we planted beans. Then... I came here and ate khichdi."

"Beans!" Ammi said through the static. "Tell me the beans part again."

qa.q: What did Rehana plant at school?
qa.a: She planted beans.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling at the start of the call?
qa.a: She felt rushed and flustered, wanting to say everything at once while the line kept breaking.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta Aunty help Rehana tell her day?
qa.a: She gave a small prompt to start with the morning, which helped Rehana put her day in order.

qa.q: What is it like for Ammi hearing Rehana's story on a bad line?
qa.a: She is far away on a night shift, so hearing about Rehana's day, especially the beans, likely makes her feel close to her daughter.

grounding: Shows a young child describing her day in sequence despite a bad phone line and an absent parent.

passage:
"Why do leaves fall down, Naveen Sir?" Bidisha, five, held up a dry leaf in the school garden.

"Because the tree lets them go in winter."

"Why does it let them go?"

"To save water."

"Why does it need to save water?"

Naveen laughed. "Because winter is dry here. What do you think?"

Bidisha frowned. "So the tree is thirsty. Like me after running!"

"Something like that." She ran off to collect more leaves, still asking the other children why.

qa.q: What was Bidisha holding when she asked her question?
qa.a: She held up a dry leaf in the school garden.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's chain of "why" questions suggest about her mind?
qa.a: It suggests she is curious and wants to understand the causes behind things, not just the first answer.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that encouraged her thinking?
qa.a: He answered simply and then asked what she thought, which let her connect the idea to her own experience of thirst.

qa.q: How might the other children be affected by Bidisha's questions?
qa.a: They may get curious too and start asking and wondering why themselves.

grounding: Shows a young child at school asking repeated causal questions and a teacher supporting them.

passage:
I'm Ritu, Vijay's big sister. I'm ten. My brother is five and asks "why" about a hundred times a day.

Yesterday we saw a rainbow. "Why is it there?" Because of rain and sun. "Why does rain make colours?" I didn't know. "Why don't you know?" I felt annoyed, honestly.

Then Mummy gave him a glass of water by the window, and a little rainbow appeared on the wall. Vijay went completely quiet. Then he whispered, "Why is it so small?" I laughed. He's always thinking.

qa.q: What made a little rainbow appear on the wall?
qa.a: A glass of water by the window, which Mummy gave to Vijay.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Vijay kept asking why?
qa.a: She felt annoyed, especially when he asked why she didn't know, but she later laughed at his curiosity.

qa.q: What did Mummy do well with Vijay's questions?
qa.a: She let him see the answer for himself with a simple experiment instead of only explaining.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu to have a brother who asks why all the time?
qa.a: It can be tiring and she may feel put on the spot, but she also admires how much he thinks 🙂

grounding: An older sister observes her little brother asking chains of why questions about how the world works.

passage:
Monday: Swati Dadi taught Payal, five, a short evening prayer. Payal mixed up the lines and giggled.

Thursday: They said it together while lighting the lamp, clapping on each beat. Payal got the first two lines alone.

Next Monday: Payal stood before the lamp, folded her hands and said the whole prayer, swaying to its rhythm. Then she started teaching it to her teddy, line by line. Swati Dadi pretended not to watch, smiling.

qa.q: Who taught Payal the evening prayer?
qa.a: Swati Dadi taught her.

qa.q: Why might Swati Dadi pretend not to watch while smiling?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy but did not want to make Payal self-conscious while she practised with her teddy.

qa.q: What helped Payal remember the prayer?
qa.a: Saying it together each evening and clapping on the beat gave her repetition and rhythm to hold the words.

qa.q: What would change if Swati Dadi had scolded Payal for mixing up lines?
qa.a: Payal might have felt embarrassed and lost interest, instead of giggling and trying again.

grounding: Shows a young child memorising a prayer through repetition and rhythm over about a week.

The school's microphone had stopped working, and Kunal, five, had to recite his rain poem to two hundred parents without it. The generator was roaring outside.

He stood on the stage, knees shaking. Zainab Ma'am, his teacher, knelt in the front row and tapped her palm softly, the way they'd practised.

Kunal watched her hand. "Rain, rain, on the roof..." He found the beat, and the words followed. He shouted the last line so loudly that everyone clapped. He ran off grinning.

qa.q: What did Zainab Ma'am do in the front row?
qa.a: She knelt and tapped her palm softly, the way they had practised.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling as he stood on the stage?
qa.a: He felt nervous, with his knees shaking, because there was no microphone and a big audience.

qa.q: Why did Zainab Ma'am's tapping help Kunal remember?
qa.a: The beat they had practised brought back the rhythm of the poem, and the words followed the rhythm.

qa.q: How might Kunal's parents feel watching him?
qa.a: They would probably feel nervous for him at first and then proud when he shouted the last line.

grounding: Shows a young child recalling a memorised poem through its rhythm despite a broken microphone.

passage:
Note from Chandrika, class teacher, Tuesday:

Pranav, five, sat alone at the sand table this morning. Last month he'd have thrown the sand. Today, when I asked, he said, "I am sad because Papa went to Pune for work and I can't hug him."

What I did next: I told him that was a big feeling and thanked him for telling me. We drew a picture for Papa together, and I told his mother at pickup so they could call Papa tonight.

qa.a: He went to Pune for work.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling, and how did he show it this time?

qa.q: How did Chandrika support Pranav once he named his feeling?
qa.a: Chandrika thanked him for sharing it, drew a picture for Papa with him, and told his mother so they could call Papa.

qa.q: How might Pranav's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She may feel touched to know he is missing his Papa and glad he could explain his sadness in words.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child naming a feeling and its reason instead of acting it out.

passage:
In the potters' lane of their village, Shalini, five, had shaped a small clay pot all morning. Her brother Dhruv, running past, knocked it off the plank. It cracked.

Shalini's face went red. She raised her hand to hit him, then stopped. "I am angry because you broke my pot!" she shouted.

Dhruv froze. "I didn't mean to."

Their grandmother wiped her clay hands. "You said it well, Shalini. Now, Dhruv, what can you do?"

Dhruv brought fresh clay and sat beside her.

qa.q: What did Dhruv knock off the plank?
qa.a: He knocked off Shalini's small clay pot, and it cracked.

qa.q: How can you tell Shalini was very angry but managed it?
qa.a: Her face went red and she raised her hand to hit him, but she stopped and said why she was angry instead.

qa.q: What did the grandmother do that helped both children?
qa.a: She praised Shalini for using words and asked Dhruv what he could do, guiding them to a repair.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv when Shalini shouts at him?
qa.a: He froze, suggesting he felt shocked and sorry, since he hadn't meant to break the pot.

grounding: Shows a young child in a village naming her anger and its cause instead of hitting.

passage:
"He took my car!" Hemant, five, stamped his foot, fists clenched, face red.

"You're really angry," Kalyani said, kneeling. "Want to do dragon breaths?"

"No!"

"Okay. I'll do them." She breathed in slowly and blew out long, like smoke.

Hemant watched. Then he breathed in too, and blew out hard. Once, twice.

"Better?" she asked.

"A little." He leaned against her. "Can I have a hug?"

"Always." After a minute he went back to ask his cousin for a turn.

qa.q: What kind of breaths did Kalyani suggest?
qa.a: She suggested dragon breaths, breathing in slowly and blowing out long.

qa.q: How did Hemant's feelings change during the scene?
qa.a: He started very angry and stamping, then calmed a little with breathing, and wanted comfort, asking for a hug.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani's approach work even when Hemant said no?
qa.a: She did the breathing herself without forcing him, so he could copy her when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Hemant's cousin see him when he comes back to ask for a turn?
qa.a: The cousin may feel relieved to be asked politely instead of being shouted at.

grounding: A home dialogue shows a young child settling anger with breathing and a hug before returning to the problem.

passage:
Note from Elizabeth, reception teacher, Thursday:

During the fire drill today, Tanvir, five, froze and began to cry when the alarm rang. After we got outside, he went straight to the quiet corner with the cushions, where he has chosen to calm down before. He hugged the big cushion and counted his fingers, as we practise.

What I did next: I sat nearby, didn't rush him, and told him the alarm was only practice. After a few minutes he rejoined the line himself.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir go after the fire drill?
qa.a: He went straight to the quiet corner with the cushions.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when the alarm rang?
qa.a: He felt frightened, freezing and crying when the loud alarm started.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do that let Tanvir settle himself?
qa.a: Elizabeth stayed close without rushing him and reassured him the alarm was only practice, so he could use his own calm-down routine.

qa.q: How might other children see Tanvir going to the quiet corner?
qa.a: They might learn that it is normal to need a calm space and that it helps someone feel better.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child using a quiet corner, a hug and counting to settle fear.

passage:
"Six! My turn again!" Ganga shouted, grabbing the dice.

"No, you had your turn," Manjula said. "It's mine."

Ganga held the dice behind her back. "But I want to win."

"If you cheat, it's not a real win."

Ganga pouted. Then she slowly handed the dice over. "Okay. Your turn."

Manjula rolled a two. Then Ganga's snake came, and down she slid. Her lip wobbled. "I lost."

"Play again?" Manjula asked.

Ganga sniffed, then nodded. "I'll be yellow this time."

qa.q: What number did Manjula roll?
qa.a: Manjula rolled a two.

qa.q: What did Ganga want when she held the dice behind her back?
qa.a: She wanted to win so badly that she was tempted to take an extra turn.

qa.q: What helped Ganga give the dice back?
qa.a: Manjula calmly explained that cheating is not a real win, which helped Ganga accept it was not her turn.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel when Ganga agrees to play again?
qa.a: Manjula probably feels happy that the game can continue and that Ganga accepted the loss.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young child accepting turn-taking and a game's result without cheating.

passage:
Note from Tenzin, football coach, Saturday:

Sachin, six, wanted to take every penalty in practice today. When I said it was another child's turn, he kicked the grass and said it wasn't fair. I asked him to count how many kids were waiting. He counted and went quiet. Later his team lost the mini-match. He was upset but shook hands with the other side.

What I did next: I told him it's hard to wait and hard to lose, and he did both well today 👍

qa.q: What did Sachin want to do in practice?
qa.a: He wanted to take every penalty.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when told it was someone else's turn?
qa.a: He felt it wasn't fair and was frustrated, kicking the grass.

qa.q: What helped Sachin accept his turn?
qa.a: Tenzin asked him to count how many children were waiting, which helped him see the fairness himself.

qa.q: How might the other team see Sachin shaking hands after losing?
qa.a: They would likely see him as a good sport, even though he was upset.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young child learning to wait his turn and accept losing fairly.
